title: Yaakov of Kfar Neburaya
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He is cited in the Yerushalmi, Yevamot ch. 2, halakha 6, and Kiddushin ch. 3, end of halakha 12, as having happened to come to the city of Tyre, where he ruled that one may circumcise a gentile on Shabbat. Rabbi Haggai heard of this and had him flogged, and he said: "חכים חביטך דהוא טבא בקילטא [wording unresolved]." This episode is likewise cited in Bereshit Rabbah, beginning of chapter 7, and in Tanhuma, Chukat, section 15, where it is also cited that he ruled that fish require ritual slaughter, and for this too R' Haggai flogged him. And in the Yerushalmi, Shabbat ch. 19, halakha 5, that he asked R' Haggai: "Then if a child is born at twilight, is he circumcised at twilight?" He said to him: "If you and I were entering through one gate, could we possibly time it precisely?" And in Berakhot ch. 8, halakha 6, he taught before R' Yirmeya; and in Midrash Shmuel ch. 7, section 6, that he preached in the synagogue of Merodata of Caesarea, and R' Yitzhak ben Eliezer was there, and the rabbis praised him. And in the Yerushalmi, Bikkurim, end of ch. 3, he preached against those who are appointed to judgeships through money, and in Berakhot ch. 9, halakha 1, he said: "The remedy for everything is silence." He is sometimes mentioned under the name 'man of Kfar Neburaya.'

notes.text: The supplied phrase חכים חביטך דהוא טבא בקילטא remains difficult. The named Yerushalmi Yevamot2:6 instead begins חבוט חבטך and ends בקולטא; it does not warrant treating Hyman’s phrase as a clear literal “wise blow in a cloak.” The English marks that wording as unresolved. ע״ז in the next sentence means “for this too,” not idolatry.

They support a comparison of the circumcision and fish episodes and the local Rabbi Haggai title. The first Haggai occurrence in the Yevamot account has that direct support. The separate Tanchuma and Shabbat Haggai occurrences retain R', as do Yirmeya and Yitzhak in the other uninspected passages; Eliezer remains untitled. Full titles in the primary passages are not transferred to those other occurrences. Yaakov and the place-name spellings in the supplied heading/body and the two digital witnesses remain distinct, without a new person/place identity binding. They may suggest acceptance of correction, but neither establishes the exact meaning or a corrected reading of Hyman's supplied חכים חביטך דהוא טבא בקילטא. That supplied wording and its unresolved marker remain in the body. The proposed resolution and mixed-note revision are not applied; the existing note and all four original mixed notes stay exact in their versions. The source's for this too is not an idolatry ruling. The printed notice (volume II, p. 772, continuing between columns on the same page) confirms the supplied חכים חביטך דהוא טבא בקילטא. It has not been corrected to the different wording of the parallels. Bereshit Rabbah 7:2 speaks of striking and learning, while the consulted Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 2:6 has חבוט חבטך and a different final word. They provide a context of accepting corrective flogging, without establishing a certain word-for-word translation of Hyman’s difficult phrase; its unresolved marker remains. The complete consulted Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 19:5 passage supports both questions about twilight and the inability to time entry precisely, rather than an assertion of successful timing. The printed Midrash Shmuel locator is chapter 14, beside the supplied/adopted chapter 7, section 6. The whole digital Midrash Shmuel 7:6 does contain the sermon in Merodata of Caesarea and the Sages’ praise; it names Yitzchak bar Rabbi Elazar beside Hyman’s Yitzhak ben Eliezer. The supplied wording and locator remain, with this witness difference disclosed. This does not establish a new person or place identity. The historical goy/noy and citation-reconstruction accounts above have not been retroactively turned into new correction history. Other exact Tanchuma, Kiddushin, Berakhot and Bikkurim loci remain uncollated here; the tentative “taught before,” the criticism of paid judicial appointments and the force of the saying about silence are retained.
